title: Deeds without measure (Mishnah Peah 1:1)
hookLine: the morning service lists things with no limit: honoring parents, kindness, hospitality, visiting the sick

cards: Almost everything in a life of practice has a size. So many minutes of prayer. So many words in a blessing.
A tenth of the harvest. Rules like that are a gift: you know when you've done it. But early in the morning service, many prayer books include a passage that goes the other way.
It names a handful of things and says: these have no measure. It's a short list, and it starts in a farmer's field.

teach.b: The passage is the opening of the Mishnah, tractate Peah: these are things that have no measure.
First, peah, the corner of the field. The Torah tells farmers to leave the edges of their fields unharvested for the poor and the stranger, and never says how big the corner should be.
Then the first fruits, and the pilgrim's offering at the Temple. Then gemilut chasadim, acts of loving-kindness. Then the study of Torah.
The rabbis later set a minimum for the corner, one sixtieth of the field, and no maximum.

Then the prayer book adds a second list, from the Talmud, tractate Shabbat: things whose fruit you enjoy in this life, while the principal stays for the world to come. Honoring your father and mother. Acts of kindness.
Visiting the sick. Helping a bride marry. Walking with the dead to their burial.

Making peace between people. And it ends: the study of Torah is equal to them all; one reading says that's because study leads to doing. Why so early in the morning, close to the blessings for waking?
One reading: the morning has just given thanks for eyes and legs and strength, and here's what they're for.
The Jerusalem Talmud adds a careful note: giving money has limits, so you don't impoverish yourself, but kindness done with your own body, your time, your presence, has none.

how: Many prayer books place the Mishnah Peah passage and the list from tractate Shabbat right after the blessings over Torah study, so that each morning begins with a little learning about kindness.

games.q: you're a farmer at harvest. the Torah says to leave the corner of your field for the poor. how big a corner?
games.why: the Torah gives no size. the Mishnah lists peah first among things without measure; the rabbis set a minimum of one sixtieth, and no ceiling.

practice: Let the list pass slowly: honoring a parent, a guest, someone sick, someone grieving, two people who aren't speaking. Notice which one brings a real name to mind, and stay with that person.
Picture the smallest version of the deed: a call, a visit, a meal, a sentence that might make peace.

wordCard.voice: Peah. The corner of a field, left unharvested for the poor — one of the deeds the Mishnah says have no measure, no set size at all.

orig.note: Hebrew: they have no measure, the opening of Mishnah Peah.

carryVoice: Your line: no limit on kindness. Money has limits; your time and presence don't. Day five hundred forty-seven, done.
